html:
In 1908 the Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda found that glutamate gives kombu seaweed broth its savoury taste. He named the taste umami and began making monosodium glutamate (MSG) to sell as a seasoning.

Ikeda, a professor at Tokyo Imperial University, wondered why dashi, the broth of kelp at the base of Japanese cooking, tasted the way it did. He extracted glutamic acid from the kelp and argued that its taste was separate from sweet, sour, salty and bitter. He patented a way to make MSG, and a business partner launched it in 1909 under the brand Ajinomoto, "essence of taste".

MSG spread through Japan, China and the rest of Asia, and later into processed foods worldwide. It became a staple of the instant noodle and the Asian restaurant kitchen. Fears about MSG in Western countries from the late 1960s were not borne out by later studies.

Western scientists took a long time to accept umami. Taste receptors for glutamate were found around 2000, and it is now widely counted as the fifth basic taste.
